This is Harry Edison; May 24th, with Stanley Dance.
Were your parents not musical, did you say?

No, there wasn't anyone in the family musical but me. I had an uncle that raised me from the time I was five until I was twelve. He had an interest in music. Not professional but he just liked music and he used to -- he'd see an old instrument out in the garbage or anything; he'd pick it up and repair it, shine it up and would bring it home. That was in Kentucky. I was born in Ohio.
When were you born? Is that date correct?

That date's correct. There's a lot of statements in the books --the jazz dictionaries, that are somewhat false because they were misinformed about my past. I was born October 10, 1915, Columbus, Ohio. My father was Hopi Indian and my mother and father separated when I was about six months old. So, you know, it's the old story, the mothers are the stalwarts of the house, you know. Years ago the women kept things together. They were very strong and instead of the man running the house the women really dominated the house. So my mother's mother became my babysitter, my grandmother. And at the age of five my grandmother died, she passed, and my mother had no one to look after me at the time because she worked very,
very, very hard. She had two jobs. One job was only paying $2.00 a week and the other, she worked part-time at night, she made $1.50 a week. So she worked very, very hard.
And after my grandmother passed, as I said, she had nobody to look after me. She sent me to Kentucky to my uncle and aunt.
Now, that would be her brother?

My mother's mother's sister. It was my great -- he was a relative of mine through marriage. His name was Robert Ward, And my mother's mother's sister, she was living in a little place called Beaver Dam, Kentucky, that's about 90 miles from Louisville.
How do you spell that?
B-e-a-v-e-r.
Oh, Beaver Dam.
Yeah, remember the tune I wrote for Basie called 'Beaver Junction.' That was -- I staved there from the time I was 5 until I was 12.
Did you know your father at all? Do you remember him?

Not really. Not really. I saw him about once or twice. Once when I was about 7 years old and I still have a vivid picture of him, you know, of how he looked. He was a very handsome guy, very, very, very handsome man.
I want to come back to that Indian thing
because, you know, it's amazing how many -- everybody talks about jazz as the Negro -- but there's a tremendous Indian thing. Did you know Duke was part Indian?
No kidding? No, I didn't know that.
On his father's side.
No kidding?
Never said much about anything else.

Yeah, well, it comes out in later years because people get inquisitive. You know, they want to know your past, your bloodline, your roots. So my mother's folks were named Schultz, S-c-h-u-l-t-z, and that's certainly not a name that's befitting to the blacks, you know, Schultz.
No, it's German.

German, yeah. And they were all mixed up, you know. In fact, there was a little city in Kentucky, there were so many Schultzs there they named it Schultztown. That was my mother's parents. And during that span of time in Kentucky, my uncle was a coal miner and a farmer, you know. Everything that we ate, everything that we accumulated, so far as the house was concerned, was grown, you know. And I worked so hard there, Stanley, I swore when I went to be a man I'd never work again.
What sort of work did you do?
Farm.
On the farm. Physical.

Physical, oh, gee whiz. You know, it's like the -- it was an old comedy team years ago, comedian named John Mason. He was a funny man. He said he never did like the farm because there were too many "ups" on it. You get up every morning -- he wasn't kidding. It was a hard job. But I had to hoe the garden, I had to plow, had to feed chickens. Oh, there's so much work to do.
Bad it was, it might have been a good thing because physically you stayed in remarkable shape.

Oh, yeah. I am very grateful, you know, for all the get-ups, the ups that I had on the farm. Because it taught me, you know, that it's good to work for what you get. There's a better way of accumulating things in life instead of going out and getting it any other way but an honest way, you know.
What sort of things did you grow?
Oh, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, corn, oh, everything, sugar cane.
You marketed all this stuff?

We ate it, mostly, because times was hard at that time, you know. Gee whiz, he was working all day long. He'd get up like 4:00 o'clock in the morning and I would have to get up first, make the room warm, make the fire, you know.
In a sense, you were a little beholden?
Oh, sure. That's for sure.
You weren't their child.
That's for sure. Then he would go -- I think he made something like $12.00 a week working in the coal mines.
What would that be worth now, $100.00?
Absolutely. Because you could get a candy bar for a nickel. Clothes was very cheap. You know, everyone grew their own, whatever they had.
........ (Simultaneous talk)
Oh, certainly. Then I would plow. I had a paper route on a horse. And then I would have to play something for him everyday. Everyday. He taught me the scales on an organ, old pumping organ.
Oh, yeah, you said he was the guy who got the old instruments. And he did know music?
No, no. He just picked it up, you know.
Well, did he have any books?

Yeah, he would send away for books, you know, just like the mail order. The mail order at that time. He would send away for different marches and he was always trying to form a band there among the youngsters. And he did have a band among -- not younger guys, some of the older guys in a little country town like to play, you know. We'd march, we'd go to different little country towns in Kentucky like Bowling Green, Owensboro, Hartford. We went as far as Indianapolis, Indiana, which is not far from Kentucky. It's a bordering
state to Kentucky, is Indiana.
How big would this marching band be?
Oh, sometimes it would be about 10 of us, sometimes it would be about 12. It was a little small community. So --
But you got started on the trumpet right away?
No, I started on the organ.
Oh, the organ.

One of the old pump organs. Remember the old organs you used to pump with your feet? Yeah. Then my ant played organ in church and I finally played organ good enough to play in Sunday School. Then I played piano.
But no real tuition?

No, no. It was a task for me to play. Because, you know, like all youngsters, everybody else is out playing football, they're playing baseball or whatever sport the kids would get enthused in. I would be in there practicing or playing something I could play for my uncle when he came in from the coal mines.
Well, you didn't need sport from the point of view of exercise because you had that.
Oh, yeah, working on the farm, that's enough exercise for anybody. But I would have to do it early in the morning before I'd go to school. I had to get up around

5:00 and school would start at 8:00. In those days, school was from 8:00 until 4:00. 8:00 in the morning until 4:00 in the afternoon, you know. 8:00 to 12:00, 12:00 to 1:00 you'd have lunch and from 1:00 to 4:00. Then I'd come back at 4:00 o'clock in the afternoon and I would still do some work in the garden, you know. And I would study and he would come in. I could always tell when he was on his way because I could hear the horse hitting a little bridge to my farm, you know. And then I would have to get enough water to feed the horse. Oh, I worked hard, Stanley. Really worked. But it was interesting. Very interesting life.
If I had it all over -- to do again, I wouldn't want to change a thing.
Did you sort of realize then how hard it was or not? Or did you sort of --
No, I didn't realize how hard it was then because it was -- you know, when kids have to work, it's hard anyway.
But it was like the norm?

It was just a normal way of growing up for any family all over the world. I wasn't any different than any other child that had parents that were farmers. Of course, naturally nowadays you can't get a kid to get up to go to school, let alone to go to work, you know. But in those days I had no choice because my uncle was the -- he was the lord and master
of his house, you know. Whatever he said, that's what he meant, you know. And it was a fantastic way of growing up. Then I finally started playing the trumpet.
Now, how'd you come to do that?

Well, he had an old cornet laying around there and it became intriguing to me, you know. It was a York. I never will forget, an old cornet. Just an old beat up thing, you know. And he finally got the valves to working. And got me a mouthpiece. He sent away to Louisville to get a mouthpiece, you know, through the mail order catalog. And I began to play that and he taught me the scales on it. I laid that down and wanted to play trombone. So I started playing a trombone just a little bit. And in the interim, I still hadn't learned how to read too good, you know. I could play the scales and the scales were -- they were easy compared to what music is today, you know. Of course, the scales are -- that's the foundation, anyway. You never get away from basics. That is the scale. And started playing the trombone. But I finally went back to the trumpet, you know.

And we played in a band, had a little band around Kentucky that would get on this wagon and we would play for like fairs or something like that that the churches would give a fair. They would call them Chautauquas, you know. That was where they would -- every woman in the church would make a pie, this one would make a cake, this one would make potato salad. Then they would bring it -- a bazaar, like a bazaar, church bazaar, you
know. And they would bring it and sell it to --
Yeah. What is the meaning of Chataqua?
Well, that's an old Indian name for a fair.
Oh, is it? I didn't know that.
Yeah, Chataqua, that's an Indian name for -- I think it is, for a gathering, you know, a lot of people.
What sort of music would you be playing?
Just old band marches, you know. The "Washington Post" march and -- no jazz. No, no, this was just marching. Just the old band, you know.
How old would you be now?
That was when I was about 8 or 9 years old.
Well, that's not too tall.

Yeah, 9 years old, you know. No jazz. But they did have some of the Dixieland music around there, like with the banjo and the washboard, you know. Oh, man, I'd stand on the outside of a little old place, we called it a dancehall, it was just built -- just a shack, really. And they would get into some really -- they knew what was going on, you know. Did a lot of dancing.
That's where you sort of hear the rhythm.
Yeah, everybody dancing, you know. Had a

a couple of banjos and the washboard and took a tub and put a string on it, you know, on a post, they would pull it to make it in tune, pull the post. They'd have one of those, you know. Oh, it was really -- that was jazz. They had something going. They had everybody dancing, that's for sure. And it sounded good to me.
And then I used to listen to Bessie Smith records.
Did your uncle have those?

Oh, yes, yes. All the old records of the old blues singers like Bessie Smith, Blind Lemon Jefferson. Oh, all the old Blues singers we had the records of. Then I happened to hear Louis Armstrong backing up Bessie Smith. And that's when it all started. That's for me. That's the direction I wanted to go in.
So that was when I was about 11 years old, you know. And he's been my idol every since. Ever since I first heard him play behind Bessie Smith. And I think Earl Hines was playing piano.
No, not with Bessie. No, I think that was [Clarence P. Johnson] (Fred Longshaw - ed.)
Was it? Didn't he make some with Bessie Smith?
No, Earl never made any with Bessie, no.
Well, what woman singer was that him and Louie Armstrong was playing with?
Oh, they played behind that woman called -- Lillie not too good, called / Dell Christian
See you can get misinformed so easily.
Yeah. Well, she was more, you know, a cabaret singer than a blues singer, really.
Did Lil Armstrong ever play behind Bessie?
Not to my knowledge.
Well, anyway, I knew that was Louie Armstrong.
Yeah. You know, Fletcher Henderson accompanied Bessie and --
That's who it was.
And James P.*
That's who it was, Fletcher. Fletcher Henderson.

But then I began to -- this was the way that I wanted to go. And then I caught a rare disease when I was about 11 -- about 10 years old there, typhoid fever. And they had no antidote for that at that time.
That's very serious.
Very serious.
Don't you get that from water?
I can imagine so, because I used to swim a lot in those old ponds, you know. There was no swimming pool. Just jump in the pond, then, on the way home from school you just
* Ed- Both Louis Armstrong and James P. Johnson recorded with Bessie Smith but not on the same sessions. However, Armstrong did accompany Smith with Fletcher Henderson, May 26, 1925.

pull your clothes off and just jump in the pond, you know. More than likely I caught it out of that. And oh, I was deathly ill. Deathly ill. In fact, the doctors there in Kentucky, he just finally gave up, you know, said there's nothing he could do, you know. And my mother came from Columbus, Ohio. And I was absolutely just burning up from the fever, you know. And my grandmother, who was my mother's mother's sister's mother -- it was my great-great-grandmother, she lived to be 108 years old, she said, well, she would use her last resort for medication. She got some fresh cow manure and made a tea out of it.
Tea?
Tea. And they gave me that tea, all day long.
It must have tasted pretty awful.

I was delirious anyway, I didn't know what it was. So that night, my fever began to come down. It began to come down. And naturally, I had to almost learn to walk all over again because I had no strength at all when I finally did come out of the coma, you know. My mother said she was just -- there was just no hope, you know. Because there was no -- now they have typhoid shots, you know, they have preventives.
And also, they have things to give you to build you back.
Sure, sure. They didn't have that in those days, you know. So that night, my fever broke. So the

doctor was just absolutely amazed. And then I think the trumpet was a body-builder for me after that, I really do. Because, you know, it's one of the finest exercises you can take for your lungs, blowing trumpet. Exhaling and inhaling, because when you breathe your lungs expand you know, really. When you're playing the horn. And your heart is good because you exercise your heart, you know.
So then I resumed playing the trumpet again.
Well, did the doctor think that the manure tea had anything to do with it?

Well, he knew it did, because whatever he gave me wasn't doing any good, you know. So -- well, and my grandmother was giving me the herbs, you know. They would dig up roots, you know, and make teas out of it. And it done more good than the medicine.
Extraordinary.

Yeah. I tell people that and it's amazing. But like it's strictly from the earth, like the cow eats the grass and there must have been something in the grass that the cows eat, you know, that was good for the fever, or whatever.
Well, there are things that people have found out over a long period of time.
Oh, sure. You know, like penicillin.
Yeah, that's right.
Sure, it's the mold off of the bread,

you know. And my grandmother used to get it off of jars of fruit that they would can or they would have canning seasons in Kentucky, you know, you canned everything. Nothing was wasted. Nothing was wasted, you know. And they would put it away in the smoke house for winters. And the mold would get on some of the fruit. And if you had a sore or a cut or something, they would go in and take the lid off of the fruit and take the mold and rub it on the sore and in a couple of days you would have a scab on it, you know, it would heal.
Astonishing. I never heard that before.
Yeah, that's what it is, the mold.
They would collect the mold off of jam or bread?
Yes, yes, off bread, you know. And that's what the medical profession says that penicillin is, you know.
And tobacco was something like an antidote for wounds, you know.
Yeah, they used to chew it up.

Sure. I was playing baseball one time and I used to catch. And the batter, he swung all the way around and the bat hit me in the head, you know, in my forehead. And oh, it was -- I still have the scar, it was a terrible cut up there, you know. And I went to my aunt and she sent me to my grandmother's. So she took some soot out of the stove and

filled this cut up, full of the soot. And she chewed tobacco constantly and took some of the tobacco out of her mouth, you know, put it up in there. And I'm still here, you know. It healed. It went right on and healed.

I cut that open when I was a kid in a woodwork class with a chisel. It was fairly big then. So the guy that was teaching me, he looked all around the carpentry shop and found a big cobweb and laid on it. It clotted on the cobweb. And that was a helpful thing and (inaudible).
No kidding. Well, see, I never heard of that.
Well, that's sort of like folk knowledge.
Well, they grew up with the knowledge how to survive without any help, you know, those older people.
I think, too, the physical work and everything you would do made you sort of -- you know, if you'd been a kind of city child you wouldn't have the resistance to --

That's for sure. Then I wouldn't be as orientated and as disciplined as I was. Because in the country where I was raised, there was no -- you had no repercussion when your parents whipped you. There was strictly discipline, whatever they said, that's what you had to do. There was no doubt in their mind that they were right. Now, there is a doubt in the kids' minds whether the parents are right, you know, and there's a challenge, a big challenge between children and
parents. But in those days, you were the challenger, which was the loser, at all times, you know. Because whatever they said was right.

And like kids nowadays, you put certain food on the table, they don't like this, they don't like that, you know, they won't eat it. But my aunt prepared a dinner and you had to eat it. And don't put any on the plate that you can't eat. Everything on your plate, you eat that. Every bit of it, you know.
And you were glad to get it.

Glad to get it, sure. And I had no likes and dislikes about what I ate because whatever she prepared, that's what I had to eat. Now kids, if you don't have lamb chops or hamburger and french fries, they don't want anything else. I had to eat all kinds of greens, I'd go out in the fields and pick greens, you know, dandelions were greens, just different kinds of greens I used to pick. And my aunt would take them home and whether I liked them or not, I had to eat. I had to eat what was there, you know.
And you probably ate things that were good for you.
Well, I'm still here, you know.
It wasn't junk food, bad chemicals in it.
It was fresh, too. And it wasn't -- as you say, there was no chemicals in it like they put in it today, you know.
You eat bread today, you don't know what the heck --

You don't know what's in it, you know. But my aunt made all the bread, you know. And everything was made right on the farm, everything. And the season when you would kill a hog -- I had to help do that, there were certain parts of them that was put up, like the ham was put up in the smokehouse and the meat -- you could go to the smokehouse, if my uncle didn't work for a year, we would still eat. Because she had everything there, you know. But that didn't make him stop me playing; whatever I did I would have to play something for him everyday, like some scales or play a different note or something. He just loved music.
That's extraordinary.

Yeah, he loved music. He had no formal training. And I've never had any either, you know. But what he taught me, it had to be a good foundation because I'm still thriving off of the foundation that he gave me.
But along the way did you study books and --

Well, when I got 12 years old, that was the grades in the school, I couldn't go any further in school. So my mother -- my uncle wrote my mother and told her that he would like for her to come and get me because the future had nothing for me down there but to go in the coal mines and be a hard working man like he'd been all his life. And, he says, "I've
taken him as far as I can. Now it's up to you.
He must have been a good man.
He was a fantastic old man.
Because I'm sure he didn't want you to go, did he?
No, he didn't. We rode in a wagon all day the day before I left, you know, and he just -- he was -- well, he got attached to me, you know. And my aunt was so attached to me, you know.
How many children of their own did they have?
None, they didn't have any kids.
Well, that's it.
Yeah, they didn't have any kids of their own at all. And my mother's mother's sister, they were part-Indians from the Kentucky reservation.
On both sides?

Yes, yes. My mother's -- I have pictures of her. She looks just like an Indian, you know. The lady that raised me, their names were Wodard, W-o-d-a-r-d. And they were very religious. I spent all my life in church. I never missed a Sunday in church unless I was sick. I taught Sunday school. My mother --
(End of side A, as recorded.)
-- I couldn't read that good, you know. But after I

would learn something, then I would learn it, you know, and I could play it. Then funerals, I would play the organ, you know, because my aunt was the organist of the church. So she played for just about everything, you know.
But what knowledge of music did she have? I mean, did she know --
She could play hymns.
But could she read?
Yes, she could read. Played the hymns, you know.
So she could help you?

Yeah, she could help you. She did quite a bit. But she was so busy most of the time. A woman's work in those days, as they said, is never done. She worked all day, everyday there was something for her to do. Wash, iron, clean, there was something for her to do all day long. So my uncle, really, when he would get in, he was so tired, he would teach me little things. Saturdays and Sundays was his biggest day, you know, to do what he wanted to do. Mostly it was on the farm but he would take time out, the boys in the little country town wanted to know something about music or they wanted to rehearse, he would leave the horse and the plow in the ground, you know, on the farm if they wanted to rehearse and practice. He'd leave everything, you know.
That was important.

Yeah, he loved it, you know. Oh, one of my most glorious moments, Stanley, was when I joined Count Basie in 19 -- I joined him, we played a dance in Owensboro, Kentucky, which is about 30 miles from where I was raised and my uncle and my aunt came to the dance.
Oh, they were still alive?
Oh, that was absolutely -- he just performed. He just performed. He came up on the bandstand and he told everybody, "I taught him what he's doing today. I taught him, you know.
He must have been a proud man.
Oh, he was so proud.
And he was pleased for you.
Yes, and he cried. And they came over to see me in a horse and buggy, 30 miles.
That's a long way.
Oh, yeah, Owensboro, Kentucky, yeah.
Well, then your mother did take you back to Columbus?

Oh, yes, when I got 12 years old she came and took me back to Columbus, Ohio. And there was a fantastic trumpet player at the time, a great friend of Sy Oliver's. He had a band around there named Pete France. Pete France, yes. Great man. He had a band around Columbus, Ohio. I'll tell you who was playing with the band, a guy named Paul Tyler, who was a
great saxophone player with Captain Wormack's band, you remember ever seeing pictures of a band, Captain Wormack?
No, I don't.

I'll tell you some of the guys in the band, this Paul Tyler, Sy Oliver, Jimmy Crawford and, let's see. Then Cincinnati wasn't too far, only 90 miles from Columbus, and they had a band that was originally out of Cincinnati called Zack White. Remember him?
Yeah, I've heard of him.
Zack White, yeah.
But how do you spell this Wormack?

W-o-r-m-a-c-k, Captain Wormack. He was from Buffalo. But then I became friends with this Pete France, he was a good trumpet player. And they had another piano player around they called Felix, he had a radio show. And my mother was good friends with most of the musicians around there because she used to tell everybody that her son was coming to Columbus, Ohio pretty soon, and I became friends with Pete and I still wasn't too enthused over the trumpet, even when I went to Columbus.

She bought me a horn at Gate's Music Store, it was -- oh, I think she payed for it for about five years because she wasn't paying but about 50 cents a month on it, you know, in Columbus, Ohio. I was still going to school and she bought me this trumpet so I could play in the band, the school band.
This was a new horn?
Yeah, this was a new horn. She was struggling and bought me everything new, you know.
Yeah, because the (inaudible).

Oh, that was terrible, it was an old York, you know. It was a cornet, too. And by that time, Louie Armstrong had made the trumpets popular, you know, the long herald trumpet -- not the herald trumpets but they were the -- the "peashooters" they used to call them. You know, Pops used to have one, it would be this long, and it was so pretty when he would play it, you know.

And Pete France -- I joined the school band and I still wasn't really -- hadn't made up my mind I wanted to be a musician. But my mother, she was sort of insisting because my uncle said, be sure and make him keep on playing, you know. And she tried to keep up the same image that my uncle had, you know. And she was still a widow and I was going to school. The junior high school didn't have any band but the senior high school had a band.

And I joined the band there at Central High School in Columbus. I first went out for football and that wasn't for me after a couple of tackles. I went right back and got the trumpet. Then I started playing baseball. I got a letter in school for playing baseball and basketball. I loved the sports.
That was keeping me from music because I wanted to be

a basketball player or a baseball player. I loved the sports. But to see the football games, I began to play in the band because we could get in and see the football games free, you know. So I joined the band just to see the football games. And I was getting around 14, there.

I met Sy -- Louie Armstrong was coming through Columbus at the time, all the time. And I would sneak in to hear him. And at that time they had all the big bands coming through Columbus. It was a big dance town because they had fantastic dance hall called Valley Dale, which the blacks couldn't go to but you could stand on the outside of the fence and hear the bands play, you see. Like Benny Moten would come through there and that's when I first met Ben Webster and Hot Lips Page, you know. Because I was living next door to a beautiful girl and I was coming from school one afternoon and I saw Hot Lips Page sitting on the porch talking to her, you know. At that time the musicians, oh, my goodness, they were getting all the girls.
They were glamorous.
Yes, yes. You know, musicians come into town, gee whiz, you'd have to hide your girlfriend. Beautiful. And then I decided I was going to be a trumpet player.
(Laughter.)
I decided there, if a musician could come right into town and accomplish something overnight that I'd been trying to accomplish for years, you know, because the girl was much older

than me, but I just admired her, you know. She was such a beautiful -- said, if he can come into town and accomplish in one night what I can't -- I guess she always thought I was just a fresh upstart speaking to her, you know.
Yeah. You know, a year or two (inaudible).

Yeah. But I used to love the way the musicians dressed because they had style about them in those days, you know. They wouldn't come on the street unless they looked the part of the musician. You could always tell the musician by his attire because he was always immaculate, you know, most of them were. Like Ben Webster, he was -- he had the big shoulders and the little Ceasar coats at that time, you know, with the padded shoulders. He had big shoulders anyway and when he put on the padded shoulders, man, he looked like a football player, you know. And his shoes were always shined and it was just such a pleasure to see musicians in those days. I said, that's for me. That's for me because that's the life I want to live. And especially when you can get to the girls, you know. That was an entre to a conversation with a lady that the average layman would never get to speak to her, you know. And I said, that's for me.

When Pops would come into town and he would be so sharp, you know. I remember before he -- you know, in his early days, you know the compass of a trumpet was from low C to a high C, and to play over this high C was absolutely impossible, like
Bach and Clark, they were writing, it's impossible to play over that. And here's a man that was hitting four or five tones over what they wrote that was impossible to do, he was doing the impossible.

So when he came to Columbus, Ohio the first time, my mother was a maid at the hotel downtown. And everybody loved her because she was diligent about her work and they all knew that she was working so hard to support me. So she asked the manager of the theater --
Had she not married again?
She got married shortly after what I'm getting ready to tell you.
Oh, I see.

And she asked the manager of the hotel, which was the Palace, downtown, blacks couldn't go -- we had mixed schools there but after school was out you'd have to go to your neighborhood and the whites go to their neighborhoods. But mixed school was very -- it played an important part in my life, the future, it really did. Because it gave me a sense of being with everybody.
Well, when you were at the school, you kids would all play together?
Well, we played together, had sports together. But after school was out, we had to go to the black part of town, the whites went to the white part of town. It was

segregated, you see. We couldn't go downtown to the theaters, you couldn't go to the restaurants, we had the black theater. It's the same old thing, you know, you had your -- but the schools were mixed. I was raised so I learned that everybody was the same in school. There was no difference.
But if you made friends with some white kid-
You were friends.
You were a friend in the school but when you'd get outside you can't go and play together?
That's right.
That must have struck you even then as very artificial.

It was, it was. But I had two or three white friends. We're still friends today when I go back, you know. And one friend, I used to stay at his house over the weekend, he'd come to my house and stay. So I grew up not having that complex, you know, about being black or white. I just grew up as another kid, just another man. But it did strike me that I couldn't go hear Louie Armstrong, you know.

So they were writing that his horn was a freak horn, he had a trick mouthpiece. In those days a trumpet player could fill the little hole up with chewing gum, you know, make the hole smaller, which would enable him to play higher but then he couldn't play low, you see. So Louie Armstrong was playing low and high, he was getting all over his horn, you know. So the

the symphony musicians, they wanted to challenge him, challenge him about his horn. So it was in the papers around there. I wish I could have cut them out and saved something like that because today it would be a classic to show how he had to prove to the people that he was just doing it on an old horn and an old mouthpiece. It's not the horn, it's the man behind the horn, you know.

So the symphony musicians, they came to the first show at the Palace Theater and he showed them the horn. They blew the horn. They looked at his mouthpiece, you know. And I'll never forget, I was standing backstage. The manager let me come backstage to hear Louie Armstrong. And he made an announcement that he was going to play "Tiger Rag" and since the people out there in the audience think this is a trick horn, he wished they would play it before he did, you know. So the trumpet player came up and played it and the band started out on "Tiger Rag".

I have never heard a man in my life -- he hit 200 high C's, counted them, while he was going across the stage, you know. And then he ended on a high F, that looked like the lights shattered when he hit that note.
Well, even to hit 200 of them must have been bad, really, for his chops.
Yeah, but he had phenomenal chops.
He must have.
His chops never went down. And then to

get a band in every place that he would go to, he'd travel by himself, just barnstorm, . . just tell them, "Who can play? "Who are these cats in town who are musicians that can play, just tell them to come on, you know," get four or five of them, "we're playing a dance tonight." Man, gee--my nerves I never heard anything like it.

And they had some pretty good musicians in Columbus. Had a trombone player there, his name was Archie -- oh, he played with Jim Europe's band years ago.* Fantastic trombone player. And they had a band around there that was called Earl Hood's band, Hooks, trumpet player, John Hooks. He was from Columbus. Sy Oliver was from around there at the time.
John Hooks, didn't he go to Boston?
That's right, yes. He was from Columbus.
I've heard tell he was extremely good.
Oh, he was a fantastic trumpet player.

And there was this guy named Paul Tyler, who was a good saxophone player. There was -- let's see, Crawford was from around Columbus a long time. There were some good musicians. Zack White's band used to hang around Columbus. Earl Hines hung around Columbus a lot. It was a good dance town because all of the neighboring cities in Ohio were good dance towns at that time.
How far is Columbus from Memphis?
Oh, it's quite a long ways. Columbus is further north.
Yes, I know that. I was wondering why -- you know, I always thought of Crawford as playing in Memphis but I knew Sy came from up there.

He's from Zanesville. And the Mills Brothers are from Pickaway, Ohio. They're from Ohio. Earl Warren is from Ohio. Teddy Wilson spent a lot of time in Ohio with Speed Webb, he was from Ohio. Chick Carter, Snooky Young's old boss, he's from Ohio. Art Tatum was from Toledo. There are many, many good musicians from Ohio. Eli Robertson, the trombone player, he was from around Ohio.
But see, all those bands used to station themselves in Ohio, Columbus, because they could go to Cincinnati, only 90 miles, go to Steubenville, only 60 miles.
Oh, it's like the center?
It's like the center. Cleveland was only 150 miles. Akron was only 90 miles, Dayton is only 90 miles --
(Inaudible) playing in those days?
Columbus? Well, I guess Columbus --
Compared to the other cities, I mean.
Well, it's the capital of Ohio. And it's a pretty big city, because Ohio State University is there, you know. And it's always been --
Is it as big as Cincinnati?
It's a little bigger than Cincinnati.
Oh, it is? I didn't know that.

And they have the capital there, see, the state penitentiary there, which we don't want to mention. But everything -- Columbus is pretty big, you know. And they had the Graystone Ballroom there, the had the Valley Dale Ballroom, they had another ballroom called Lane Askin's, they had another room called -- oh, there's a theater there on Long Street in the black neighborhood, the Pitian Temple, that was a dancehall, the Masonic Hall, that was a dancehall. And bands used to play around there, every night there was a different band playing.
They wouldn't be playing every night?
Yeah.
One or another?

Yeah. Well, to get in a dance then wasn't but a dollar and a quarter, you see. And I guess the highest paid musician was getting around $12.00 a night, that was a lot of money. When I first went with Basie in 1938, I was only making $6.00. $6.00 a night.
Was that seven days a week?

Seven days a week. We never had any days off. Basie was only making $15.00 and he was the bandleader. But we could get a room for like 35 cents. And if they charged you 50 cents for a room, you'd move out. That's 15 cents you could eat on the next day. You figured on 50 cents a day for your lodging and food, you see.
That's what's absurd today, isn't it, about inflation?

That's for sure. 50 cents, I remember one time Pres used to be the first one off the bus to get a room. And while we were all trying to get ourselves together, he would probably be up in the room asleep, you know. And he went to get his room and all of a sudden he came down the steps rushing and cursing. I said, "What's wrong, Pres?" He said, "The room rent went up from 35 cents to 50 cents and I checked out," you know. He checked out. That was funny, because she went up 15 cents on the room.

There was no hotel, we would stay in the private homes, you know. A woman would have a big house, a boarding house, five or six rooms. So five or six guys would stay here and then four or five would stay someplace else, you know. So -- but Columbus was sort of a mecca for the big bands in those days. They had so many. They had places downtown the whites, you know, theater.
Well, when did you start -- this was where you started playing professionally?
Yeah, that's right.
After high school?
Yeah. Well, there was a band called Earl Hood around there --
Hood or Hook?
Earl Hood, H-o-o-d. Earl Hood.
And the fellow I was telling you about, Paul Tyler, who was a

fantastic saxophone player, he -- oh, Johnny Hodges knew him well, everybody, because he was really a good saxophone player. He moved next door to my mother and I used to play and play, you know, try to be a trumpet player. So he heard me one day he said -- he was playing with Earl Hood. He said, "Why don't you come to rehearsal."

So I went to rehearsal and Earl Hood liked me so I joined the band. And we had a job on Saturday nights, you know, just around Columbus, Chillicothe, Ohio, someplace. And my mother bought me a tuxedo and everything. And, of course, we got paid, it was only about 35 cents or 50 cents, very seldom $1.00, you know. But he wouldn't pay me. He'd say, well, you're playing for experience, see.

So I'd come home, I'd be so sleepy on Monday I wouldn't have my homework done. And my mother would ask me -- well, she had gotten married then, I had a stepfather. And she would ask my stepfather, "Don't you think he should be getting some money?" He said, "Well, he's playing like everybody else." So she asked me, says, "What do you do with the money?" I said, "Well, he didn't pay me, Mom." And she said, "Well, that seems strange that you go out and work and don't get paid for it." So she said, "What did Mr. Hood say?" I said, "Well, he would tell me I'm playing for experience."
So she went along with it, you know, for a while. So she said, "Now, if you don't get paid tonight, I'm going to see

him myself."

You know, the mothers would take it upon themselves to go see whatever, they wouldn't care what it was, they would go to hell to see why your kid was being mistreated, you know. And she said, "Well, that's mistreatment. I bought you this tuxedo and you've got a new horn." And she would say, "How in the hell does he think you're going to make it in life and help me and help yourself unless you get paid? She said, "Experience, you can't eat experience, you know."

So she said, well, you just can't work no more if you are just going to work for experience. So he finally started paying me 35 cents a night. And this band was -- this guy named Archie White, trombone player, oh, he was -- everybody, Lawrence Brown knows him. He was a fantastic trombone player. Oh, he was really one of the world's greatest. You know, when you would play with Jim Europe and go to Europe with Jim, you had to be --
Technically good.

Technically, yeah, he was a good trombone player. And let's see, who else was in that band? Earl Hood's band -- oh, probably nobody that -- of any prominence that you would have heard of except Paul Tyler.
Now, the dances, what were you playing there?
Well, we were playing dance music, the same thing that -- I remember the first solo, everybody was

playing solos and finally I just started playing mine one night on 'Lime House Blues.' Everybody turned around and said, 'Who is this kid playing,' you know. So that was my debut as a soloist in a band, in any band, with Earl Hood. I started playing 'Lime House Blues.'
Were you sort of modeling it on Louie Armstrong?
Oh, definitely. Definitely. And then I played -- went to school until there was a band called Morrison's Grenadiers. They formed a band around there with Sy Oliver, Jimmy Crawford, Joe Thomas --
Oh, Joe Thomas?
Yeah, he's from Columbus, too. Joe Thomas --
The tenor player?

Yeah, the tenor player, the tenor player. Joe Thomas, this Hooks, John Hooks. Oh, I forgot who all was in that band. But anyway, they were some rich family loved music and they backed this band. And they got some of the best musicians, they called them Morrison's Grenadiers, the family was named Morrison. So they got this band together around Columbus and they went to Cleveland, and they asked my mother could I go to Cleveland. She said, 'Yes, if you go and come back and go to school.'
Well, it was supposed to have been just a job for a
short time. So I went to Cleveland with this band and music had gotten in my blood then, you know. I was only about 15 or 16 then.
Is Cleveland as big as Columbus?

Oh, yes. It was larger. Because there were nightclubs around there, man, all kinds of nightclubs. And that's the first time I met Art Tatum. He was playing at a club around there called Valson (PHONETIC) Alley in Cleveland. And him and another pianist very good at the time, Lannie Scott.
Lannie Scott went to New York, didn't he?

Yeah, he played with Jonah Jones for a long time. And they had another piano player around there named Pickett, he married the chi-chi girl, Rose Murphy. He was a fantastic player. He died. He was a good piano player. They all used to play together around there, you know. And this -- my mother came and got me and made me go back to Columbus and finish school.
And then, that's when these fellows, Je ter and Pillars came through Columbus. And --
Where did they come from, St. Louis?

No, they were from Texas. They were originally from Texas. Je ter Pillars -- they were from Arkansas. Alphonso Trent, he's from Arkansas, too. But the band got its prominence in Texas because they were the first black band to play on radio from a hotel called the Adolphus Hotel.
Alphonso?

Alphonso Trent, yeah. He had a good band. He had Snub Mosley, trombone player Snub Mosley. He had a trumpet player, fantastic trumpet player named Chester Clark. He had a good drummer called A. G. Godley. I think you've heard about him.
Yeah, I've heard of him. Peanuts Holland?
Peanuts Holland was in that band. Peanuts Holland. Oh, --
Stuff Smith?

Stuff Smith was in that band, yeah. Snuff Smith was in that band. Alphonso Trent, he got sick up in Bangor, Maine, up there, they were doing one-nighters. So he went back to Ft. Smith, Arkansas. So the band came through Columbus, Ohio and broke up. So the Jeter-Pillars was the one --, Jeter was an alto saxophone player and Pillars was a tenor player. They decided they would get the band going, you know.
They were both in Trent's band, I see.
Yes. I didn't even know Trent. Or Lacey or none of them.
So they asked my mother, could I go to Cleveland on a job. So she said yes. So we went to Cleveland and started playing at a place called the --

Yeah, that's where I met Basie's present wife, Catherine. She was a dancer in the club.
Now, when would this be?

This was around 1935. 1935, yes. And naturally, we all were youngsters at that time. We became very good friends. And I used to go around to her mother's house and she would feed me quite a bit. Mrs. Morgan.
Oh, was she from Cleveland? I didn't know that.

Cleveland, yeah. And then we started working a place that was just a hotel, called the Heat Wave Bar. This was Jester-Pillars, I was playing trumpet, Snub Mosley was playing trombone and Godley was playing drums. I forget who we had on bass. A guy playing tuba named Slim Waters. He could play tuba like you play trumpet. Oh, he used to jam with the trumpet players. He was from Jersey.
Waters?

Slim Waters. I never knew his first name. But he could play the bass like you play trumpet. In fact, we would go to work at like 9:00 and get off at 4:00 in the morning and sometimes you didn't get off at 4:00, you had to play then as long as some people were in the audience, you know. 8:00, 9:00 10:00 o'clock. Then we would go to places
and jam after that. And he would take his bass and jam with the trumpet players, you know.
So then times got pretty bad --
Well, how big was this band? Just one trumpet?
Just one trumpet. One trumpet, trombone. It had six pieces.
No piano player?

Yeah, had a piano player. Let's see, we had piano, bass, three saxophones and two horns, so had eight pieces. And finally we hired a guitar player in Cleveland named Jimmy Miller. He was -- he later married Catherine, which is Basie's wife now, you know.
Oh, really?

Oh, yeah, we were all kids together, Jimmy Miller. And then we went to -- started playing in a club -- the Morrison Grenadiers went to Cleveland, we played in a place called the Cotton Club. And then my mother came and got me and made me come back to Columbus, Ohio. Then I came back -- now I'm talking about when I went there with Jeter-Pillars. There was a piano player there that you've probably heard of named Poison Gardner.
Yes. But I don't know anything about him.
Well, he was not the undertaker. There was quite a few clubs in Cleveland that -- all over Cleveland
you could hear live music, and some good musicians there. Edward Berry was playing at a club there at the time.
Is this where he comes from?
Yes. And Tad Damron had a brother, Cesar, was a good saxophone player. He was playing there at the time.
What made Cleveland tick in those days? What was there?

Well, you know, wherever there's a lot of underworld, there's a lot of money. And at that time there was a lot of speakeasies, you know, where you could go buy whiskey, you know. And the town was flourishing because there was all those illegitimate clubs you could go to and people were having more fun then than they're having now, you know. That's where Art was playing, in a place called Valsen Alley. The man that used to serve the whiskey, you know, the old time douche bags that the women used to have and they had the rubber, you know, and the spout, he would fill that full of whiskey. Fill it full of whiskey and put it on his shoulder and walk around in the crowd. If you wanted a drink, he would just take the little spout and the whiskey would come out there in the glass.
(Laughter.)
That's how -- you'd go in Valsen Alley and he would come with this douche bag on his shoulder, you know, full of in the
whiskey, and have this long rubber hose in it.
(Laughter.)
That's not such a bad idea.
Sure did. Served a purpose.
How was Tatum playing in those days? Just the same?
Just the same.
Marvelous.
Oh, my goodness. Playing the piano out, oh, my goodness. He's been in jazz ever since I've been knowing him. Oh, this was --
A real gift.
Well, he graduated from the School of the Blind right across the street from me in Columbus, Ohio. There was a college for the blind in Columbus, Ohio on Parsons and Main, and that's where I met him.
Oh, right from when you began?
Yes, he graduated from that school, School for the Blind.
Well, when you say graduated, what would they have taught?

Oh, they taught him how to read Braille, taught him how to -- just the same as a school you would go to, all was in Braille, you know. And he learned music there and learned how to read music with Braille, you know. It was just
like any other school only it was a school for the blind. He'd always been -- he could never see good.
Well, I mean, did he get all of his musical training there?
I don't know, but he got some of it. I don't know where he got most of it because I think he was born with most of it.
Well, of course, they very often say when you lose one faculty it sharpens up the others. It may have done something like that.

Well, I would say he was born with most of his talent. But he went to school there to improve it. There wasn't too much improving he could do, but later on in years he did have more finesse. I don't know whether he had more or not because Tatum was always a genius to me. He was always good. He used to keep people in Vale's just absolutely -- the more he played the more you would drink to listen, you know. And he would play until 10:00, 11:00, 12:00 o'clock in the daytime.

Because in those days you had no hour to quit but you had an hour to start. You started at 9:00 and you left when everybody left the club. As long as they were tipping. And, you know, we were making $12.00 a week there in Cleveland and we'd have like $5.00 and $6.00 a night in tips. Had the kitty there and people would put dollar bills in there, $5.00
bills. People -- I don't know, it was just such a gay time in those days.
Well, how confident in yourself did you feel by this time? Were you playing from written music there?

Yeah, but most of it was from head, even in Alphonso Trent's band. Sy did a lot of writing in the band but it was near as complicated as the reading that you have to do nowadays. What we played in those days is like what beginners play to like what you have to play now in studios, you know.
But I was building my confidence as a soloist, you know.
(Inaudible).

Yeah, yeah. And then I'll never forget, while in Cleveland, McKinney's Cotton Pickers came through there. They had Roy Eldridge, Billy Bowen, Teddy Wilson, Teddy Wilson's brother Gus. Oh, man, what a band he had. What a band he had. And Clyde Hart was playing in the band. And this was later on, after the musicians I'd seen McKinney's Cotton Players -- seen with McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Columbus, they had a drummer, Cuba Austin, and all these guys, you know. But this is later in the years when Roy joined the band.
He came in an after hours bar one night because he used to carry his horn everywhere to play. I remember, he
almost made me want to quit. Oh, he could play. Oh, he had chops -- the only two people I ever heard who could play endlessly were Pops and Roy Eldridge.
Really?

Yeah. The longer they played, the stronger they would get. Pops just played, he could play for hours and hours and hours, all night long. And never miss a note, never crack a note or anything. Just absolutely --
(Inaudible).
Well, he had good teeth formation.
I suppose there is a secret of it.

Oh, yeah. And then he had perfect lip for playing, you know. He had a perfect lip for playing. And he was just so far ahead of his time. Absolutely just amazing how a man can pave the way 50 years ago and you're still playing some of his things, you know. I think for any trumpet player to play a decent solo, he's got to play something Pops has played, really.
I mean, even like Dizzy sort of had to revolt against something.

Yeah, sure. But he still plays some of the things Pops played, you know. He still plays some of the things Pops played. And you can call it be-bop if you want to, if that's what it was, he was playing it in the '30s. He was playing it in the '30s.
Well, it seemed to me they were playing -- well, we're jumping a bit ahead. We should talk about that later. How long were you with Jeeter - Pillars ?
Well, we left Cleveland, stayed there about a year, and went to St. Louis. Stayed there about two or three years.
Oh, didn't the band get a bit bigger then?
No. The band was just -- well, we did add another trumpet player.
Who was that?
George Hudson.
Oh, he later had a band of his own.
Yes.
What sort of trumpet player was he, like a first man?

No, no, he wasn't a first trumpet. Well, we all played first. He wasn't a strong trumpet player. And we had a trombone player named Smitty, Carter Smith, Trombone Smitty they called him. Good trombone player.
Yeah, I've heard of him.
Then after he left, Gus Wilson, Teddy's brother, joined the band. And then --
Was Gus good, too?
Oh, yes. Yes. And a good piano player. Oh, yeah. Write beautifully. Write beautifully. He was sort
At that time?
Oh, yes. Yes. Great musician.
What happened to him, do you know?
I don't know. But after A. G. Godley left the band and the bass player that we had stayed in Cleveland, we got Jimmy Blanton.
Oh? He was really young.
And Sidney Catlett.
Wow, that was a good band.
Sure. Sidney Catlett and then when Sidney went back to join Fletcher Henderson in Chicago, then Jo Jones joined the band. And Walter Page, after Jimmy left.
(Inaudible).
Yeah, and Walter Page joined the band. And then --
Who was on piano at this time?
Chester Lane, who plays here now with Teddy Buckner out to Disneyland.
Was he good?

The piano player? Yeah. Good piano player. And then Jimmy Miller was the guitar player at the time, and Catherine, they were still married, she was dancing in this club called The Plantation. And in St. Louis, we all left Cleveland to go to work there at the Plantation. And

Catherine and Jimmy, they divorced and she went back East. And Jimmy Blanton joined Duke and Basie sent and got Walter Page and Joe Jones, and that's how I got into Basie's band, through recommendation from Joe Jones and Walter Page, when I got to New York.
Oh, I always sort of wondered.
I'm working up to it.
(Laughter.)
You know, I never saw the connection.

Oh, we worked together around St. Louis a long time, Jo Jones and I. And Walter Page. And then a trumpet player, a tenor player, they added another tenor player to the band which is Gene Porter. He used to play with Earl Hines and then they had a band there who I just read in this book that they connected me with, Eddie Johnson and his Cracker Jacks. Harold Baker was playing with that band, see, and I never did play with the band. But I knew him quite well because they used to come through Columbus, Ohio. That's the first time I ever heard Tab Smith was with Eddie Johnson and Jacks his Cracker /, Tab Smith. That's the first time I heard him play.
(Millinder)
Like when you were together with Lucky.
Yeah, right. And that's who recommended me for Lucky, you know. I had known Tab in St. Louis and he had left there before them but he used to come back.
And Louie Metcalf, trumpet player.
He was out there?

Yes. They all used to play on the boat with Charlie Creath, you see. They played on the boat with Charlie Creath, which was the best job you could get in the season. And there was Sidney Catlett, he played on the boat, there was Louie Metcalf, Fate Marable, he was playing with Charlie Creath at the time. Later on he became a bandleader himself.
Where did Sidney Catlett come from?
Chicago.
Oh, I see.
He came from Chicago.
Walter Page, where did he come from?
He came from Oklahoma. He had a band called the Blue Devils. Before he joined Benny Moten he had a band called the Blue Devils.
So he came to Jeter-Pillars in between?

Yeah. Because when Benny Moten died, he came to play with -- Benny Moten's band broke up for a period of time. He came to St. Louis to play with -- well, Jeeter and Pillars had known all these guys through the years because Alfonso Trent had a good band, you know. I hear he had a fantastic band. I mean a good band, you know. So at that time, just like musicians today, like if you're with a band

and the bass player's getting ready to quit, you'd say to the band leader, let's get so-and-so. So Walter Page had been a friend of Pillars' so when Jimmy Blanton went to Duke, he said, well, let's see if we can get Walter Page, which he was living in Kansas City, which is only a few short miles from St. Louis. So we got Walter Page.
Then when -- we had a drummer named Wilbur Kirk, went to Noble Sissle's band, and that's the first time I met Lena Horne. She was a vocalist with Noble Sissle.
Wilbur Kirk, didn't he end up with that Sidney -- went to Paris?
Went to Paris, yeah. The same guy, a drummer, yeah. We got Jo Jones then. And when Basie finally reassembled Benny Moten's band to go at a place called the -- oh, this place there in Kansas City --
The Reno Club?

Yeah, the Reno Club. They all went back to join Basie. And about that time, Lucky Millinder sent a telegram to some trumpet player there in St. Louis he wanted to come but he sent tickets to a friend of mine who was playing with the St. Louis Crackerjacks. I met him with then, named Harold Arnold, he was a tenor player. So he and I were good friends. So he said, 'Well, I got a ticket here so I have to get the trumpet player Lucky sent for.' So he said, 'Why don't you take the ticket and let's both go to New York.
So I said, "Well, he didn't send for me, he sent for somebody else." So he said, "What difference does it make," you know. So, okay, we got on the train and went to New York.
So you went on spec, as it were?

That's right. And I -- well, my girl-friend who I had been going with in St. Louis, she was dancing in the Cotton Club. She left before I did. And had she not left, I guess I would have stayed there but I went following her at the time, you know.
She went where?

New York Cotton Club, yes. And it was full of chorus girls around St. Louis, testing chorus girls, you know, Claudia Oliver, that fantastic dancer. Joe "Ziggy" Johnson was producing the shows there at the time. It was a big club, you know. And all the big musicians that would come through there with Fletcher Henderson and all the other bands, they knew somebody that was in the Jester-Pillars band because they had been big musicians themselves; Sidney Catlett knew Walter Johnson who used to come through there with Don Redman, there was Fletcher -- and Walter Johnson. And I met them all because they all used to come through St. Louis, you know. And Jester-Pillars knew all these musicians from Alphonso Trent days, you know.
So this telegram came -- I forget who the trumpet player Lucky sent for, but anyway, I got on the train and I went to New York and Tab Smith told Lucky, this is a good
trumpet player. And I think I played with Lucky about six months before I joined Basie.
Oh, not longer than that?
No.
Because you made some records --
Made a few, yeah. Well, we had -- Lucky had a good band. He had Charlie Shavers, Billy Kyle, he had Tab Smith in the band, Don Byas --
Oh, Don Byas was in that band?
